text: Latin casa meant 'hut, cottage' – the humble word ousted the stately domus (kept in 'domestic'). A casino is Italian for 'little house'.
Via Old French from Frankish gard, 'enclosure' – the same Germanic fence-word as 'garden', 'yard' and the -garten of kindergarten.
Latin salire meant 'to leap' – Spanish calmed it down to 'go out'. English 'salient' and 'somersault' still take the jump.
From Latin plicare, 'to fold' – sailors folding sails at journey's end turned 'folding up' into 'arriving'. Plegar kept the fold.
Latin gustare, 'to taste' – tasting slid into pleasing. English took 'gusto' from the same root, plus its opposite, 'disgust'.
Latin incantare, 'to sing a spell over' (cantare, to sing) – charming someone is literally singing magic at them. Hence 'enchant'.
Latin furnus – Spanish softened f- to h- (as in harina from farina), while English 'furnace' keeps the Latin fire burning.
Latin traducere, 'to lead across' – meaning led across languages. English 'traduce' marched the same word into 'slander'.
Latin classis was the Roman citizenry called to arms, ranked by census – a 'classic' was classicus, 'of the first class'.
Latin mirabilia, 'things to wonder at' – from mirari (to wonder), which also gave 'miracle', 'admire' and 'mirror'.
Japanese jū (gentle) + dō (way) – 'the gentle way', the name Kanō Jigorō gave his softer school of jujutsu in 1882.
Latin quadrum, 'a square' – a painting is literally 'the squared thing'. A squad began as a square battle formation (Italian squadra).
Latin vinum – the ancient Mediterranean wine-word behind 'wine' and 'vine'. Vinegar is French vin aigre, 'sour wine'.
Latin borrowed camminus from the Celts – one of the few Celtic words on the Spanish map. French chemin walks the same road.
From Latin tendere, 'to stretch' – first the stretched canvas tent, then the market stall beneath it, then any shop.
Min Chinese te, shipped by Dutch sea trade – coastal routes gave Europe 'té' and 'tea'; the overland road spread Mandarin chá as 'chai'.
Latin populus meant the people, not the place – a village named for its inhabitants. English borrowed 'pueblo' back from Spanish.
A Germanic bench-word – moneylenders worked from benches, so the bench became the bank. Bancarrota, bankruptcy, is a 'broken bench'.
Vulgar Latin veranum tempus, 'spring-like time' (ver, spring) – Spanish summer began as late spring. English 'vernal' keeps ver.
From Frankish smalt via Old French – the same Germanic melt-root as English 'smelt' and 'enamel': glass melted onto metal.
Latin Veneris dies, 'day of Venus' – English Friday swapped in Frigg, the Norse goddess matched to Venus. Same day, different love.
Vulgar Latin hibernum tempus, 'wintry season' – the same root sleeps on in English 'hibernate'.
Latin sors, the lot you drew – fate as a lottery. English 'sort' shares it, and a sorcerer (sortiarius) was a caster of lots.
Latin gallus meant both 'rooster' and 'a Gaul' – the Roman pun outlived Rome: the cockerel is still France's national emblem.
Latin patronus, the protecting father-figure (pater) – English split it into the 'patron' who pays and the 'pattern' you copy.
Latin iocus meant 'joke' – Romance turned joking into playing and dropped ludus, the old game-word. English kept 'joke' literal.
Latin materia, 'matter, raw material' – timber was THE material. Portuguese agrees: the island of Madeira is simply 'wood'.
Latin senior, 'the elder' – respect measured in age. English 'sir' is the same word, worn down through French sire.
Latin campus, the open field – camps and campuses share it, and a champion was originally the fighter left standing on the field.
Greek plateia, 'the broad way', via Latin platea – 'place' and 'piazza' are the same street; English took 'plaza' from Spanish.
From Arabic barri, 'the outside' – the quarters beyond the city wall. English later borrowed 'barrio' back from Spanish.
A hybrid word: the Arabic article al- fused onto Latin morsus, 'a bite' – same biting root as 'morsel' and 'remorse'.
Greek idios, 'one's own' – a language as a people's own speech. An idiotes was merely a private citizen; hence 'idiot'.
Greek historia meant 'inquiry' – Herodotus sold his 'researches' as the first history. English split it into 'history' and 'story'.
Latin costa, 'a rib' – the coast is the land's ribcage. A cutlet (côtelette) is a little rib; to accost is to pull alongside.
Latin passer, 'sparrow' – in Spanish the humble sparrow's name spread to every bird. Ornithologists keep 'passerine' for perchers.
Latin femina, worn smooth – f- became h- and -mn- became -mbr-, exactly as homine became hombre. 'Feminine' is the same word intact.
Latin capsa, 'box' – 'case' and 'capsule' are kin, and 'cash' originally meant the money-box rather than the money inside.
Persian lazaward – lapis lazuli – via Arabic; the initial l- was dropped as if it were an article. 'Azure' lost it the same way.
Greek petra via Latin – 'petrify' is turning to stone, 'petroleum' is rock-oil, and the name Peter was coined to mean 'the rock'.
Latin rivus, 'stream' – rivals (rivalis) were originally neighbours sharing one stream, and to 'derive' is to draw water off it.
Latin mercatus, from merx, 'goods' – 'market' and 'merchant' trade on it, and 'mercy' began as merces, the wages of kindness.
Named after its own last line – Latin 'Ite, missa est' ('Go, it is the dismissal'). English 'Mass' and 'dismiss' share missa.
Latin kalendae, the month's first day, when debts fell due – a calendarium was originally a moneylender's account book.
Latin domina, mistress of the house (domus) – 'dame' and 'dominate' are kin, and English took 'duenna' straight from Spanish.
Late Latin spatula, 'shoulder-blade' – the blade-bone came to name the whole back. French épaule and 'epaulette' kept the shoulder.
From Latin deportare, 'to carry away' – off work, into amusement. English 'sport' is the same escape, clipped from 'disport'.
Via French galoper from Frankish – likely wala hlaupan, 'to run well'. The Germanic verb also survives in 'leap' and 'lope'.
Literally 'un-fasting': des- + ayuno (fast), from Latin ieiunium – the exact logic of English 'break-fast'.
Greek kinema, 'movement' – the cinématographe of 1895 was a 'movement-writer'. 'Kinetic' runs on the same root.
Latin insula – a peninsula is paene insula, 'almost an island', and to isolate someone is literally to make an island of them.
Latin for 'fish-pond', from piscis – Roman piscinae held fish before swimmers. The zodiac's Pisces swims in the same root.
Latin penicillus, 'little brush' – English 'pencil' is the same tool, and penicillin was named for the mould's brush-shaped spores.
Nahuatl chocolatl – the Aztec cacao drink reached Spain in the 1500s; Europe added sugar and passed the word to every language.
Nahuatl tomatl, carried home by the conquistadors – every 'tomato' on earth still echoes the Aztec name.
French chauffeur, literally 'the stoker' – the first cars were steam-driven, so the driver's real job was keeping the fire hot.
Late Latin campana, 'of Campania' – the region round Naples cast the finest bronze. A campanile still rings with the place-name.
Greek Mouseion, shrine of the Muses – Alexandria's was a research temple. 'Music', mousike, is the Muses' own art.
Greek theatron, 'the seeing-place' (theasthai, to behold) – 'theory' is the same watching, turned inward as contemplation.
Latin tormentum, a twisting siege-engine (torquere, to twist) – the storm as torture. 'Torment' and 'torque' twist alongside.
